title: Liberty and Prosperity -- Ch. 19: The Senate v. Ermita: Validity of EO 464 Barring Executive Officials from Appearing in Congress
keywords: Bengzon v. Senate Blue Ribbon Committee
Chavez v. Presidential Commission on Good Government
right to information on matters of public concern
primary_topics: Chapter 19 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' -- a digest of Senate v. Ermita, in which a unanimous 14-0 Supreme Court, through Justice Conchita Carpio Morales, upheld Sections 1 and 2(a) of Executive Order 464 as pertaining to the discretionary Question Hour but struck down Sections 2(b) and 3 for unduly curtailing the congressional power of inquiry in aid of legislation.

The constitutional distinction the ruling turned on: Section 22 of Article VI (the Question Hour, where the appearance of department heads is discretionary and requires presidential consent) versus Section 21 (inquiries in aid of legislation, where attendance is compulsory because the power of inquiry is coextensive with the power to legislate).

The doctrine of executive privilege as the Court delimited it -- a constitutional but narrow and exceptional exemption attaching to certain sensitive types of information, never to officials merely by reason of their office, which must be formally and clearly invoked by the President or by the executive secretary 'By order of the President.'

The procedural gateposts the Court resolved first -- the standing of the Senate and its members, of the party-list representatives and of Bayan Muna, the denial of standing to PDP-Laban, and the ripeness of the controversy -- together with the denial with finality of both Motions for Reconsideration and Justice Tinga's Separate Opinion grounding EO 464 in the President's power of executive control.
sub_topics: The facts: on September 28, 2005 the President issued EO 464, effective immediately, requiring heads of departments to secure presidential consent before appearing before either House and defining the nature, scope and coverage of executive privilege.

Section 2(b) enumerated who were covered -- senior executive officials, generals and flag officers, PNP officers of chief superintendent rank or higher, senior national security officials, and such others as the President might determine -- each by the judgment of their respective superiors.

Invoking EO 464, executive and military officials declined to appear at Senate hearings in late 2005 and early 2006 on allegations of presidential electoral fraud, irregularities in the North Rail project, and the misuse of fertilizer funds.

The senators claimed EO 464 virtually rendered the Senate inutile, and the Senate and several senators filed consolidated Petitions for Certiorari and Prohibition invoking Article VI, Sections 1, 21 and 22, and other provisions.

The three synthesized issues: whether EO 464 contravened the congressional power of inquiry, whether it violated the right to information, and whether respondents gravely abused their discretion by implementing it before publication.

Standing: the Senate and its individual members had a substantial and direct interest and could sue to keep their legislative prerogatives inviolate; party-list representatives Ocampo, Casiño, Virador, Beltran, Mariano and Maza, and the national party-list group Bayan Muna with its three House seats, likewise had standing.

PDP-Laban, not a party-list group, had no standing: its claim that EO 464 hampered its legislative agenda was vague and uncertain and at best a 'generalized interest,' whereas concrete injury is an indispensable element of a justiciable dispute.

Ripeness: EO 464 did not require a deliberate withholding of consent or an express prohibition, and since its implementation had already produced nonappearances it would have been sheer abandonment of duty for the Court to refrain from passing on its constitutionality.

The Question Hour: the Constitutional Commission's framers treated Sections 21 and 22 as distinct, and the present Constitution removed the mandatory character of appearance during the Question Hour to conform to a presidential system -- so Sections 1 and 2(a) of EO 464, which referred only to Section 22, were upheld.

Inquiries in aid of legislation: Sections 2(b) and 3 were invalidated because, per Arnault v. Nazareno, the power of inquiry is coextensive with the power to legislate and grounded on the necessity of information to the legislative process.

Limits on the inquiry power: per Bengzon v. Senate Blue Ribbon Committee an inquiry may not usurp judicial functions, is subject to certiorari review, must follow duly published rules of procedure, must respect the Bill of Rights, and should indicate the subject and the questions involved.

Executive privilege defined: Schwartz, Rozell and Black's Law Dictionary were quoted, U.S. v. Nixon was recounted as recognizing a constitutionally allowable but defeasible privilege, and Almonte vs. Vasquez was cited for the presumptive privilege for presidential communications.

The principle that emerged: executive privilege is recognized only in relation to certain sensitive types of information, its validity depends on the ground invoked and the context, and its extraordinary character inclines heavily against executive secrecy and in favor of disclosure.

Exemption from inquiry: only a valid claim of privilege exempts department heads, never their status as such; only the President is absolutely exempt, being reachable only through impeachment, and members of the Supreme Court are exempt on separation-of-powers, fiscal-autonomy and judicial-independence grounds, a point Senate counsel Joker Arroyo conceded upon the Chief Justice's interpellation at Oral Argument.

How the claim must be made: clearly asserted with a statement of its specific basis, though Congress must not demand such particularity as to compel disclosure of the very information protected, the privilege against self-incrimination offering a useful analogy.

Why Section 3 in relation to Section 2(b) was invalid per se: it virtually allowed the President to authorize claims of privilege by mere silence, leaving Congress woefully unable to judge whether withholding was justified; the power to invoke is limited to the President, or to the executive secretary acting 'By order of the President.'

The reasonable-time rule: a summoned official must be given time to inform the President or executive secretary of a possible need to invoke, and if neither invokes after a reasonable time, Congress may compel the appearance.

Right to information: EO 464 concerned only congressional demands, not citizens' demands, which lack the obligatory force of a subpoena duces tecum -- yet because legislative investigations are generally public, any issuance unduly limiting disclosure there denies citizens access to matters presumed of public concern.

The Motions for Reconsideration: non-publication of the Senate's inquiry rules had no bearing on EO 464, which rested solely on executive privilege; the 'for practical purposes' tentative prevention was rejected as speculation; and PDP-Laban was distinguished from Bayan Muna on party-list representation and seat-forfeiture grounds, both Motions being denied with finality on July 14, 2006.

Justice Tinga's Separate Opinion: EO 464 was really a set of instructions under the presidential power of executive control and valid on its face, since even without it the President could order officials not to appear; but its actual application produced unconstitutional consequences, and the Decision stood as a vital precedent for the standards it laid down.

notable_anecdotes: At the Oral Argument the Chief Justice interpellated Senate counsel Sen. Joker Arroyo, who admitted that members of the Supreme Court are likewise exempt from legislative inquiry -- a point the Decision records as not in dispute.

The chapter recounts the American parallel: in U.S. v. Nixon the President was ordered to produce the Watergate tapes, and although the U.S. Supreme Court found a confidentiality privilege constitutionally allowable despite no explicit textual basis, it rejected Nixon's specific claim after balancing it against the public interest in the fair administration of criminal justice.

Officials invoking EO 464 simply stayed away from Senate hearings into presidential electoral fraud, the North Rail project and the fertilizer funds -- the concrete nonappearances that made the Court treat the case as ripe rather than premature.

Respondents argued on reconsideration that the ban was 'for practical purposes,' since the President could not object to a question the instant it was asked; the Court answered that a tentative prevention rests on mere speculation that the information might be confidential, and Congress cannot be bound by so tenuous an invocation.

PDP-Laban protested that it was no different from Bayan Muna, whose standing had been upheld; the Court answered that its congressmen were elected in their individual capacities for their districts and would not forfeit their seats on changing party, unlike Bayan Muna's representatives.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 19 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' digests The Senate v. Ermita, the challenge to Executive Order 464, which the President issued on September 28, 2005 requiring department heads and a broad class of senior executive, military, police and security officials to secure presidential consent before appearing before either House of Congress. Invoking it, officials declined to attend Senate hearings on alleged presidential electoral fraud, the North Rail project and the fertilizer funds, and the Senate and several senators sued, claiming the order had rendered the chamber inutile. In a unanimous 14-0 Decision written by Justice Conchita Carpio Morales, the Court first upheld the standing of the Senate, its members, the Bayan Muna, Anakpawis and Gabriela representatives and the Bayan Muna party-list group, while denying standing to PDP-Laban for asserting only a generalized interest, and held the case ripe because implementation had already produced nonappearances. On the merits it distinguished Section 22 of Article VI, the Question Hour, where appearance is discretionary under a presidential system, from Section 21, inquiries in aid of legislation, where attendance is compulsory because, per Arnault v. Nazareno, the power of inquiry is coextensive with the power to legislate. Sections 1 and 2(a) of EO 464 were therefore sustained, while Sections 2(b) and 3 were struck down. Drawing on Schwartz, Rozell, Black's Law Dictionary, U.S. v. Nixon and Almonte vs. Vasquez, the Court held that executive privilege covers only certain sensitive types of information, never officials by reason of office, and that its extraordinary character inclines heavily against secrecy and in favor of disclosure. A claim must be clearly asserted with its specific basis stated, may be invoked only by the President or the executive secretary 'By order of the President,' and cannot be made by mere silence; an official summoned must be given reasonable time to seek an invocation, failing which Congress may compel appearance. The Court also noted that unduly limiting disclosure in public legislative investigations denies citizens information presumed of public concern, denied both Motions for Reconsideration with finality on July 14, 2006, and recorded Justice Tinga's separate view that the order was valid on its face as an exercise of executive control though unconstitutional in its application.
